Performance retention & stability measures

Each metric has its own aggregate value and workload-average retention score. Each configuration is normalized to its own first workload level unless an explicit reference is selected. Native measurements, loss under load and frame-time dispersion remain available below.

One value per metric

The retention score is average retained performance across the full workload range. A score of 90% means this metric retained 90% of its reference performance on average across that range. Each metric also has an aggregate value in its original units.

Scores use the area under each metric’s retention curve divided by the workload span, with straight lines between adjacent measured levels. Actual workload spacing determines the weights. Compare scores over the same range, coordinate and reference. Values above 100% remain possible.

FPS lows are reciprocal frame-time percentiles: 1% low = 1000 / p99(ms); 0.1% low = 1000 / p99.9(ms). A 0.01% low would require p99.99. The aggregate averages each load’s low-FPS statistic; it is not a percentile of pooled frames. An end-to-end rate describes net loss and can hide intermediate rises and falls; the curves below retain that detail. Single-point runs and incomplete curves have no full-range score. Native SD/CV aggregates retain their own units.

2configurations
66recorded laps
1.1.0formula version
Reading the curves. Retention is P/P0 for FPS and T0/T for frame time. Degradation is 100(1 − retention); negative degradation means improvement. Local degradation rate is the change in degradation divided by the actual load interval. Its points sit at interval midpoints. A slope near zero can occur at either high or low absolute performance.

Native per-lap measurements are summarized as equal-lap arithmetic means. Ratios and slopes are calculated afterward. Whiskers in this section are approximate 95% cluster-bootstrap intervals, not frame-level sampling errors. One run resamples whole sweeps; multiple runs resample whole runs. Fewer than 3 independent units: no inferred interval. 3–9 units: exploratory interval. Identical cluster support is required across dependent loads. The reference retention of 100% is an algebraic identity, not a claim of zero measurement uncertainty.

Within-lap frame-time dispersion

Within-lap SD and CV describe frame-time distribution spread. They are not chronological predictability measures. Between-lap variation above describes repeatability of the selected lap statistic; its SD is distinct from uncertainty in the mean.

ConfigurationReference loadReference average FPSReference lapsReference selection
Demo-A12103first_manifest_workload_for_configuration
Demo-B11653first_manifest_workload_for_configuration

Timescale changes simulation speed and capture duration. It is a native workload coordinate, not a chicken-count equivalent or a verified amount of completed simulation work.

Average FPS

Higher retention indicates less loss relative to this metric’s reference; it does not imply higher absolute speed. A 1% low measures a distribution tail and is not a complete measure of temporal consistency. Lines stop at missing or invalid levels. See the table for sample counts and uncertainty availability.

1% low FPS (reciprocal p99 frame time)

Higher retention indicates less loss relative to this metric’s reference; it does not imply higher absolute speed. A 1% low measures a distribution tail and is not a complete measure of temporal consistency. Lines stop at missing or invalid levels. See the table for sample counts and uncertainty availability.

Higher retention indicates less loss relative to this metric’s reference; it does not imply higher absolute speed. A 1% low measures a distribution tail and is not a complete measure of temporal consistency. Lines stop at missing or invalid levels. See the table for sample counts and uncertainty availability.

Higher retention indicates less loss relative to this metric’s reference; it does not imply higher absolute speed. Higher retention indicates less loss relative to this metric’s reference; it does not imply higher absolute speed. Higher retention indicates less loss relative to this metric’s reference; it does not imply higher absolute speed. A 1% low measures a distribution tail and is not a complete measure of temporal consistency. Lines stop at missing or invalid levels. See the table for sample counts and uncertainty availability.

Within-lap frame-time SD

Higher retention indicates less loss relative to this metric’s reference; it does not imply higher absolute speed. A 1% low measures a distribution tail and is not a complete measure of temporal consistency. Lines stop at missing or invalid levels. See the table for sample counts and uncertainty availability.

Within-lap frame-time coefficient of variation

Higher retention indicates less loss relative to this metric’s reference; it does not imply higher absolute speed. A 1% low measures a distribution tail and is not a complete measure of temporal consistency. Lines stop at missing or invalid levels. See the table for sample counts and uncertainty availability.

Within-lap frame-time dispersion

Within-lap SD and CV describe frame-time distribution spread. They are not chronological predictability measures. Between-lap variation above describes repeatability of the selected lap statistic; its SD is distinct from uncertainty in the mean.

Definitions & limits

Reciprocal retention for lower-is-better metrics expresses throughput-equivalent performance loss. A latency increase of 100% corresponds to 50% retention, not zero retention. It is not the same as percentage latency increase. Negative degradation and retention above 100% are preserved.

Aggregate scores use uniform weighting in the native workload coordinate and trapezoidal integration. Different metrics and sweep modes are reported separately. Slopes depend on native workload units, baseline, and interval size; they are observed secants, not a continuous derivative. Small adjacent differences can be noisy. Confidence intervals do not model systematic drift or workload-count error.

Hardware/configuration labels are supplied by the user. Endpoint chicken counts are consistency checks, not verification of every moment of the capture. The original report section retains its historical calculations; this section can exclude additional laps when metric sample support or metadata contradicts the workload.
